title: Node failure recovery and hot-swap runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This runbook is a draft operational guide for handling node-level infrastructure failures that affect GPU-backed inference capacity. It covers immediate on-call actions, safe cordon/drain procedures, hardware hot-swap guidance, cluster recovery steps, and add-capacity flow when replacement capacity is needed quickly.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Kubernetes clusters hosting inference pods (GPU nodes) and the dedicated GPU pools in Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Assumes on-call SRE has access to cluster admin credentials, Terraform/cluster provisioning pipelines, and hardware contact points for colo/cloud vendor.
- Hardware-level hot-swap instructions are vendor- and site-specific; this doc contains generic safe steps — always follow the colo vendor's checklist if available.

Roles & contacts:
- Primary on-call: triage, runbook execution, Slack incident channel.
- Hardware contact: vendor-level technician for physical GPU replacement/power-cycle. 
- Infra ops lead: approves capacity-add or emergency reserved allocation.
- Owners: eng-sre (Ava Martinez), infra-ops (Ravi Patel).
- Slack channels: #sre-oncall, #infra-hardware (escalate to vendor triage).
- Pager escalation: SRE pager -> infra lead -> CTO (per escalation policy).

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm alert: check PagerDuty alert, Prometheus/Alertmanager details (node-exporter, kubelet, GPU Exporter metrics).
2) Identify scope: is it single node or multi-node? Check: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady / taints.
3) Check pod impact: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep <node-name> to see affected inference pods.
4) Gather logs: kubectl describe node <node-name>, journalctl -u kubelet -b, dmesg | tail -n 200, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log (if present).
5) Short-lived vs persistent? If node flapped, consider cordon/drain. If hardware GPU error (ECC, nvlink errors), open hardware ticket.

Immediate safe actions (recommended order):
- Step 0 (communication): Create incident channel (#incident-<short-id>) and Jira ticket (SRE-incident template). Post initial status to #sre-oncall with severity and node name.
- Step 1 (isolate): kubectl cordon <node-name>  # prevents new pods from scheduling
- Step 2 (evacuate): kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=60
  - If drain hangs because of pods stuck in Terminating, kubectl describe pod to find finalizers; consider delete --force as last resort with approval.
- Step 3 (verify): kubectl get pods -o wide on replacement nodes; confirm pods have restarted and passed readiness checks.

Diagnosing GPU-specific failures:
- Check GPU visibility: ssh to node and run nvidia-smi -q and nvidia-smi topo -m. If nvidia-smi times out or fails, likely driver/hardware issue.
- Inspect kernel logs: dmesg | egrep -i "gpu|nvrm|nvidia|ECC|GPU fault"
- Check GPU exporter metrics (node-exporter + nvidia-dcgm): if DCGM reports GPU unreachable or NVML errors, tag as hardware.
- If errors show ECC or persistent memory faults, escalate to hardware vendor immediately.

Hardware hot-swap (high-level, vendor-dependent):
NOTE: If this is a cloud-managed instance (GCP/Azure/AWS) follow cloud provider hot-swap/replace instance flow instead of physical instructions below.
- Prepare: Document node hostname, instance id, serial numbers, last-used migrations. Attach current logs to ticket.
- Power down procedure: follow vendor-provided SOP. Typical safe sequence: cordon & drain -> power off node -> remove GPU (or schedule tech to replace) -> reseat / replace -> power on -> validate BIOS sees card -> verify driver loaded (nvidia-smi) -> uncordon.
- If device replaced, check CUDA and driver versions: nvidia-smi shows expected driver; run a small inference smoke test (run minimal model container) to verify inference GPU path.
- If vendor requires RMA, tag node with RMA id and avoid reusing GPU until validated.

Cluster recovery and capacity add (if replacement will be delayed):
- If immediate capacity is needed and cluster has spare pool: scale up instance group / node pool via autoscaler or Terraform: terraform apply -var 'node_pool=gpux-large' -target=module.node_pool
- If Dedicated reserved pools are exhausted, request emergency reserved capacity from infra-ops: escalate to infra lead (Ravi).
- Route traffic to compatible model variants or lower-resource models (policy: degrade to quantized model with same API) — coordinate with product and solutions-eng.
- For temporary cloud instances: provision pre-baked GPU node image from images/gpu-worker-ami-2026-01 and join cluster: use provision script /usr/local/bin/join-node.sh <token>.

Validation checklist after node returns or capacity added:
- NodeState: kubectl get nodes and ensure Ready (STATUS).
- GPU presence: ssh -> nvidia-smi; verify all GPUs present and in expected state (no ECC flags).
- Pod readiness: kubectl get pods -A | grep model-serving; ensure readiness probes pass for 2 consecutive checks.
- Telemetry: check Per-route latency dashboards for 15m window to ensure no regression.
- Cost: if we spun up emergency capacity, annotate Jira ticket and tag usage for cost center reconciliation.

Rollbacks and backout plan:
- If new node/image causes regressions, cordon and drain the node, and deprovision via Terraform: terraform destroy -target=module.node.<instance-id>.
- Revert to prior machine image by reprovisioning previous AMI or rolling back infra change MR.

Post-incident: RCA and follow-ups:
- Owner: on-call SRE to prepare initial timeline within 24 hours and assign RCA lead within 72 hours.
- Required RCA sections: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, detection gap, mitigation, long-term fix, test plan.
- Example artifacts to attach: kube logs, dmesg, nvidia-smi output, vendor RMA response, Terraform plan diffs.
- Suggested next steps (examples): enable stronger GPU health metrics (NVLINK/ECC alerts), add automated node replacement playbook, maintain spare capacity buffer on Dedicated pools.

Runbook testing & maintenance:
- Quarterly tabletop drills: simulate node failure with cordon/drain; time to restore should be measured.
- Validate drain scripts and forced-delete policies in staging before using in prod.
- Owner (Ava) to review this doc every 6 months or after every Sev1 node incident.

On-call notes (real-world tips & gotchas captured during incidents):
- "Don't force-delete model pods immediately — they often recover on other nodes if cordoned early."
- "If a GPU is intermittently visible (nvidia-smi works intermittently), it's almost always hardware flakiness — escalate early to avoid wasted operator time."
- "Cloud preemptible GPUs can look like hardware failures — check instance lifecycle events in cloud console."
- "When draining, watch for local-volume pods; they need special handling and may extend downtime if deleted incorrectly."

Commands quick reference (examples):
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=60
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- ssh core@<node>
- sudo journalctl -u kubelet -b --no-pager | tail -n 200
- dmesg | egrep -i "nvrm|nvidia|gpu|ECC"
- nvidia-smi -q
- terraform plan -target=module.node_pool
- terraform apply -target=module.node_pool

Slack incident initial post template:
- Subject: [INCIDENT] GPU node failure - <cluster> / <node-name>
- Body: On-call SRE <name> triaging. Node <node-name> NotReady/Driver error. Pods drained: <count>. Severity: P2 (adjust if impacting customer latency). Current action: cordoned+draining; opening vendor ticket. Channel: #incident-<id>.

Jira ticket template summary: "Node <node-name> GPU failure - <cluster> (YYYY-MM-DD)"
Description fields:
- Detection time:
- Symptoms (alerts):
- Immediate actions taken:
- Hardware ticket RMA / vendor notes:
- Attach logs: list of files and snippets

Open items / TODOs for doc (draft):
- Add step-by-step vendor-specific hot-swap checklist for Equinix/Packet and bare-metal partners.
- Add exact Terraform targets used for each environment (staging/prod).
- Add automated post-drain sanity checks (kube-probe smoke test).
- Define SLO for node replacement time for Dedicated pools.

Notes to self (Ava):
- Coordinate with Ravi to get spare GPU reserve policy for Dedicated customers.
- Add automated alert that correlates GPU-exporter errors + kubelet flapping to reduce false positives.

End of draft runbook.
